text:
In the Provincial Court of Alberta

Citation: R.
v. Weekes, 2010 ABPC 274

Date:

20100819

Docket:
100507045P1-01-001, 002

Registry:

Calgary

Between:

Her Majesty the Queen

-
and -

Ancel Peter Weekes

Reasons
for Judgment by the Honourable T.C. Semenuk

Introduction

[
1
]

The Accused is charged with criminal harassment and uttering a
threat. There has been no election or plea to the charges by the Accused. The
Crown has brought an application pursuant to
Section 672.23
of the
Criminal
Code
,
to have the Court render a verdict pursuant to
Section 672.31
of the
Criminal
Code,
that the accused is unfit to stand trial. For the reasons that
follow, I find the Accused fit to stand trial.

Facts

[
2
]

The Accused is charged in an Information as follows:

Count 1:    Between the 1
st

day of July, 2008, and the 28
th
day of April, 2010, both dates
inclusive, at or near Calgary, Alberta, did without lawful authority and
knowing that John Vos is harassed or recklessly as to whether John Vos is
harassed, engage in repeatedly communicating with either directly or
indirectly, John Vos or anyone known to them, that caused John Vos reasonably,
in all circumstances, to fear for their safety or the safety of anyone known to
them, contrary to
Section 264(2)
(b) of the
Criminal Code of Canada
.

Count 2:    On or about the
26
th
day of April, 2010, at or near Calgary, Alberta, did knowingly
utter, convey or cause Cst. Mark MacDonald (RCMP), to receive a threat to cause
death or bodily harm to David Ruthorford, contrary to
Section 264.1 (1)
(a) of
the
Criminal Code of Canada
.

[
3
]

At the hearing, the Crown called one witness, Dr. Xie, a Forensic
Psychiatrist, and expert in mental disorders. The Defence called no evidence.

[
4
]

Dr. Xie
, whose qualifications were admitted by Defence
Counsel, testified in examination-in-chief, that the Accused came to the
forensic unit on May 5, 2010, for assessment as to his fitness to stand trial.
She determined that he was suffering from a mental disorder, schizophrenia,
paranoid type, chronic and treatment resistant. He also suffered from
hypertension and high cholesterol. He was taking prescription medications to
control his various health problems.

[
5
]

The mental disorder suffered by the Accused is a most severe
disorder mainly characterized by thought disorder and delusions. His affect was
flat and he had behaviourial problems including violence, impaired judgment and
lack of insight.

[
6
]

The delusions were of the persecutory type that involved mood swings,
impulsive behaviour and little insight by the Accused into his mental condition
and his need for treatment.

[
7
]

The Accused had been refusing treatment, but since he was certified
under the
Mental Health Act,
on May 21, 2010, he has been receiving
compulsory treatment by way of injection of antipsychotic medication, called
Consta, which is a form of Respiridol. He is also given Respiridol oral pills,
2 milligrams at bedtime. Unfortunately, the Accused stopped taking the pills
and only takes the injections.

[
8
]

The original dosage of treatment for the Accused has been
increased from 25 milligrams to 37.5 milligrams, to 50 milligrams, every two
(2) weeks.  She hasn’t seen much change in the Accused other than he is a
little bit mellower and not so angry or aggressive.

[
9
]

She prepared a nine-page report as to the fitness of the Accused
to stand trial, dated June 25, 2010, and it was marked in evidence as Exhibit 1
in the first stage of the proceedings. After the Accused was certified under
the
Mental Health Act
, he cancelled his appeal of that decision.

[
10
]

According to the Accused’s history, he has been suffering from a mental
disorder for many years and has numerous admissions to the psychiatric unit since
2004. He has always been diagnosed with schizophrenia.

[
11
]

The Accused has paranoid delusions. There are mainly two parts.
One is the grandeurs part. He believes that he is a high ranking military
officer in charge of lots of things with a lot of power. He also believes that
he is a Senior Advisor for Alberta Health Services and has done many
investigations for the Health Region. He believes that he is a computer genius
and has revolutionary ideas that were being stolen from him in his home. He
believes that he has millions or billions of dollars coming to him and he
promised many people that he would build a new medical building clinic in High
River. He believes that he was going to be sent to Ottawa as a high ranking
supervisor from Alberta, but has changed his mind because communication with
the Queen is difficult, and there are political reasons. He also has
persecutory delusions such as a computer device being set up in his house above
his bed and in the walls. He believes the radio host complainant  involved in
the charges before the Court is connected with the persecutory conspiracy to
get his ideas on computer software. He tried to buy the radio station so they
would not do this to him. He also thinks the treatment is persecution. He has
sued two doctors at the Foothills Hospital, and believes they got 100 years in
jail and their licences were suspended. He believes that Dr. Xie, will get 100
years in jail, if she continues to give him medication.

[
12
]

Taking his medication has proven difficult because he believes that it
will cause him to have a heart attack. He believes the only medication he needs
is a sleeping pill called Immovane.

[
13
]

As a result of his delusions, the index offences involve the Accused
allegedly harassing and making threats to a local radio personality named
Ruthorford, on radio station QR 77, in Calgary. He told her that he informed
the police of his intention to go to a public place to confront Mr. Ruthorford.
He made threats, but he was not actually going to harm or hurt Mr. Ruthorford.

[
14
]

The Accused also believes that the manager at the Safeway store
where he worked, hired a Jewish spy agency to plant listening devices in his
house in order to steal his revolutionary ideas about computer software. He
believes they planted similar devices at the Foothills Hospital and also in his
car. He believes that Safeway has obtained a house key from a locksmith and
that his ex-manager, has stolen some equipment from his house and hurt his
little dog. He also believes people are following him when he leaves his house, and sometimes he carries a baseball bat
with him.

[
15
]

She does not believe the Accused understands the nature or
objective of the criminal  proceedings that he faces. He does not understand
his charges. He often requests his immediate release from the forensic unit. He
often says there is an order from the Queen or from Ottawa to release him
immediately. He doesn’t think his harassment was serious, that he had a right
to do what he did, and he was going to plead not guilty. There is a possibility
he will do this further in the future, confront people, but he would never hurt
them physically.

[
16
]

She does not believe that the Accused understands the
consequences, if he were to be convicted. His understanding was very poor. He
doesn’t think he will be found guilty and he will be released quickly.

[
17
]

She does not believe that he is able to assist in his own defence. He
has fired many lawyers. His thought process is loose and disorganized and he
cannot really focus in order to  communicate with Counsel.  He is so
delusional, he believes he is a really important person with lots of power to
do things. Based on his past experience in firing so many lawyers, she
questioned his ability to advise Counsel properly.

[
18
]

Her prognosis was that the Accused was not likely to improve.
Because of his lack of insight, poor compliance with treatment, and given his
age of 67 years with potential heart problems, high cholesterol and
hypertension, they cannot force him to take a higher dosage of medication.

[
19
]

Usually, improvement is seen after six weeks’ of treatment. The
Accused has been treated for eight weeks without any noticeable improvement.
He hasn’t shown any change in his delusional thoughts, although he is generally
pleasant and calm. His prospect of being fit for trial is not foreseeable in
the future. It may improve in a couple of months, if more aggressive treatment
is administered to the Accused at the Edmonton Hospital.

[
20
]

On cross-examination, Dr. Xie testified that individuals
suffering from paranoid schizophrenia are resistant to treatment, and if
discharged, the Accused is likely to stop taking his prescription medication.
In fact, the Accused is refusing to take pills at the forensic unit, requiring
the dosage for his injections to be increased. More aggressive treatment would
be possible at the Edmonton Hospital. The facility there is better equipped to
handle any emergency situation. She agreed that the Accused’s concern over a
heart attack, if the dosage was increased, was a possibility.

[
21
]

According to the Accused’s history, when he was at the hospital
in Ponoka in 2006, he was taking the prescribed medication by injection every
two weeks and he was good, almost symptom free, and he stayed on the medication
for two more years until 2008. Then he deteriorated, refusing his medication,
and had multiple admissions. If he complies with the treatment, he will improve
quickly.

[
22
]

In order to make the Accused fit to stand trial, he needs more
medication so he will not be so delusional.

[
23
]

Although there are past reports from family members and medical
reports of the Accused carrying a baseball bat, because he was being followed
by strangers, the Accused has never hurt anyone, and he has no criminal record
related to violence. She agreed that the Accused was not physically aggressive
or intimidating to her. For the most part, he was pleasant and calm.

[
24
]

As to the nature of the proceedings, she agreed that the Accused
understood the charges that he is facing, and the procedure, but believes that
the charges have already been dropped. He didn’t think what he did was wrong,
he intends to plead not guilty, and the matter was not serious. He believes
that he was being kept in the hospital and improperly detained.

[
25
]

She agreed that somebody could have delusions and still be fit to
stand trial. She also agreed that it was not uncommon for people with mental
health disorders not to have insight into their mental health status. This is
particularly the case with people diagnosed with untreated schizophrenia.

[
26
]

She testified that she saw the Accused every week at the forensic
unit. She agreed that she never asked the Accused whether he understands the
charges he is facing, and stated, “Well, he knows he’s having the charge of
harassment”. He also understands that he is being charged with harassing the
radio station and with uttering threats to Mr. Ruthorford.

[
27
]

As to the consequences of the proceedings, she talked to him about his
understanding if the judge convicts him. His response was that, he thinks he
will be found not guilty of the charges. He thinks the charges will be dropped
and he will not be convicted, so she didn’t pursue that any further.

[
28
]

In terms of communicating with Counsel, she agreed that she only knew
that the Accused fired one lawyer.

[
29
]

On re-examination, Dr. Xie testified, that she was not aware of
any record of anyone suffering a heart attack from taking Respiridol, however,
it depends on the dosage of every medication and the individual’s physical
condition, so there is a possibility.

[
30
]

On being questioned by the Court, Dr. Xie testified, that she
spoke with the Accused the day before the hearing, and he told her that the
charges against him will be dropped.

Issue

[
31
]

Should the Court, pursuant to
Section 672.31
of the
Criminal
Code
,
render a verdict that the Accused is not fit to stand trial?

Law and Analysis

[
32
]

Recently, this Court in
R. v. Iyoho,
2009 ABPC 262
,
had occasion to canvass many of the reported decisions dealing with the legal
principles to be applied in a fitness hearing such as this.

[
33
]

It is not my intention to repeat what I said in that case, other than
to adopt those legal principles where they may apply in the particular
circumstances of this case.

[
34
]

In
Iyoho
,
supra
, this Court found the
accused unfit to stand trial on all 3 grounds, stated in the definition of
unfit
to stand trial,
found in
Section 2
of the
Criminal Code
.
He too
was suffering from a mental disorder diagnosed as schizophrenia-paranoid type,
with grandiose and persecutory delusions.

[
35
]

I see many distinctions between
Iyoho,
supra,

and the case at bar.

[
36
]

Firstly
, the Accused in the case at bar, did not interrupt the
fitness hearing, as the evidence was being adduced. Unlike
Iyoho,
supra,

the accused in the case at bar, did not give the appearance by his demeanor
in Court of someone suffering from a severe mental disorder.

[
37
]

Secondly
, the Accused in the case at bar, was very
discreet in terms of quietly consulting with Defence Counsel as the evidence
unfolded. Furthermore, he instructed Defence Counsel to admit Dr. Xie’s
qualifications as an expert witness, and during the adjournment, after Dr. Xie
had testified, and after consultation with Defence Counsel, elected to call no
evidence at the hearing.

[
38
]

Thirdly
, unlike the accused in
Iyoho,
supra
,
the Accused here understands the
nature and object of the proceedings

he faces. According to the evidence given by Dr. Xie, he understands the
charges he is facing and the procedure. He knows he is charged with harassment
and uttering a threat. He knows these charges relate to his allegedly harassing
a local QR 77 radio station personality named Ruthorford, and uttering threats
to him. He maintains that he didn’t do anything wrong, and intends to plead not
guilty. The day before the hearing, he told Dr. Xie, that the charges will be
dropped.

[
39
]

Fourthly
, unlike the accused in
Iyoho,
supra,

the
Accused here understands the
consequences of the proceedings
. Dr.
Xie talked to him about his understanding if the judge convicts him, although
she didn’t put the question to him directly. His response was that he thinks he
will be found not guilty of the charges, or they will be dropped. She didn’t
pursue the matter further.

[
40
]

Fifthly
, unlike the accused in
Iyoho,
supra,
there
is no evidence before me that the Accused had any difficulty
communicating
with Counsel
. Dr. Xie assumed he was having difficulty because, from
what she was told, the Accused fired a number of lawyers. As it turns out, he
discharged one lawyer and by his conduct in Court, had no apparent difficulty
communicating with Defence Counsel during the hearing.

[
41
]

I accept Dr. Xie’s evidence, that the Accused suffers from a mental
disorder diagnosed as paranoid schizophrenia, with grandiose and persecutory
delusions. That being said, Dr. Xie testified that somebody could have
delusions and still be fit to stand trial. The cases support this conclusion.

[
42
]

In
R. v. Rooney,
(1994) P.E.I.J. No. 82 (PEISC)
, Jenkins,
J., at para. 37,  held that it cannot be said that an accused is unable on
account of mental disorder to conduct a defence, if he is able to recount the
necessary facts relating to the event in such a way, that he can properly
present a defence. If that ability is presently blocked by delusions caused by
a mental disorder, then an accused is not fit to stand trial.

[
43
]

Having heard and considered all the evidence in this case, I am
not satisfied on the balance of probabilities, that the Accused’s ability to
recount the facts is blocked by any delusions he may have according to Dr.
Xie’s evidence

[
44
]

I am also not satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that the
Accused lacks a

limited cognitive capacity,
to understand the
process and to communicate with Defence Counsel. His thought process may be
loose and disorganized and he may not, because of his delusions, be capable of
exercising analytical reasoning in making a choice to accept the advice of
Counsel or in coming to a decision that best serves his interests, but as
pointed out by the Supreme Court of Canada, in
R. v. Whittle,
(1994)

1994 CanLII 55 (SCC)
, 2 SCR 914, per Sopinka, J., at para. 33, that is not a prerequisite.

Ruling

[
45
]

The Crown has failed to satisfy me on the balance of
probabilities, that the Accused is unfit to stand trial.

Dated at the City of Calgary, Alberta, this 19
th

day of August, 2010.

T.C. Semenuk

A Judge of the
Provincial Court of Alberta

Appearances:

A.W. May

for the Crown

Ms. J.L. Ruttan

For the Accused
